intro.title: The story behind my résumé
intro.text: I grew up in Vernal, Utah, and I have spent an extraordinary amount of my life being interested in things that, at first, seem unrelated: theater, government, technology, community, business, and the strange work of persuading people to make something together. This is the story behind those interests, not just the list of jobs they produced.

sections.title: The kid who rooted for the inventor
sections.subtitle: Childhood · Vernal, Utah
sections.preview: There is a particular kind of movie character I've always loved: the one who makes everybody else groan when they announce they have an idea. Usually their first attempt is a disaster. Sometimes their second attempt is worse. But they're not content to leave the world exactly as they found it. I find that enormously appealing. I also recognize a less flattering part of myself in it. I can become so excited about what something *could* be that I underestimate the amount of actual work involved. My experience with an enormous school arch would eventually provide a very expensive education in that difference.
sections.expanded:
I have never found inventors interesting only because they make clever things. The wonderful part is what happens before the invention works, when the idea sounds ridiculous and the person holding it is the only one who can see what it might become. I love that uncomfortable gap. I love the makeshift prototype, the notebook full of sketches, and the moment another person begins to see the possibility too. That is the part of the story I remember long after I have forgotten how the machine works.

Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs is hilarious to me because Flint Lockwood takes his imagination so seriously. His ideas are enormous, impractical, and usually catastrophic before they become useful. Meet the Robinsons carries a similar affection for the strange little people who keep inventing even after they have made a mess. A Bug’s Life has another idea I have always loved: one small person with an apparently silly invention discovers that people can change their circumstances when they decide to do something together. I came to tick, tick… BOOM! later, as an adult. Its urgency about making something meaningful before time passes speaks to a part of me that was shaped much earlier.

I am not claiming I was a child prodigy drawing revolutionary patents in my bedroom. I was an imaginative kid who was fascinated by what people could dream up. I liked plays and stories because they gave an audience permission to believe in something different for a while. I liked projects because the imaginary thing had a chance to become tangible. The line between the two still feels thin to me. A stage set, a community archway, a banking app, and an event platform all begin with somebody being willing to picture a thing before it is there.

There is something especially funny about growing up with that kind of imagination in a town like Vernal. I love the place, and I still do. It is far from the places people usually imagine when they think about major technology companies or monumental art. But people in a small town can be astonishingly resourceful. You learn who has a welder, who knows somebody at the city, who can lend a truck, who might make a phone call, and who will bring their own tools because the idea sounds good. A lot of the large things I have been involved with started in exactly that way.

The stories that stay with me are full of stubborn optimism. They also acknowledge that being imaginative can be lonely. Sometimes people laugh at the idea. Sometimes the whole project goes sideways. The interesting characters find their way back to it. I suppose I have spent a good portion of my life trying to do the same. I still want to know what could happen if someone tried.

sections.title: Life Is Short
sections.subtitle: Ages eight to ten · Vernal, Utah
sections.preview: I don't want my father's death to swallow the story of my childhood. He was alive for the years I got to know him. He taught, coached, went to games, came home to us, and had a life that wasn't just the illness that ended it. I think that's one reason I've kept returning to the stories his students tell. Each one gives me another small piece of a person I was too young to know fully. And it reminds me that the most important parts of a life aren't always the things that fit neatly into a biography.
sections.expanded:
My dad's name was Shanon Johnson. He taught computers at our high school and coached basketball. He was the sort of teacher people kept finding years later to tell him what he had done for them. As a child, I did not have language for all of that. I knew he was my dad. I knew he went to school and games and that people seemed happy to see him. It took years, and hundreds of conversations with people who had known him, to appreciate how deliberately he had made other people part of his life.

When I was eight, our parents called a family meeting. I had been in the basement watching television and knew something was unusual as soon as we were asked to come upstairs. Our family did not usually gather with that kind of seriousness. My two older sisters and I sat together while our parents tried to explain cancer to children who had no real concept of what it meant. I knew the word was frightening. I had no idea what the next two years would feel like.

Dad continued teaching and coaching during treatment. In a piece I wrote about him later, I remembered how he scheduled chemotherapy around school and basketball, trying to return in time for games. I remembered him insisting on walking the school stairs, and I remembered the pain he carried home. There were days he would retreat into the darkness because light hurt his head. Yet he still found energy to care about students who were struggling and to work on the little projects that kept his children inspired. The effort looks almost impossible to me now that I am older.

For a while, he seemed to beat the cancer. We were allowed to imagine that our lives had returned to normal. Then it came back. I was with him for a medical visit when the news emerged, almost by accident, that his illness had returned. That second diagnosis changed everything. We knew time was narrowing, although I cannot pretend that an eight- or ten-year-old understands time the way an adult does. I remember people visiting, one after another, and the strange feeling that everyone was trying to say goodbye without having to use the word.

He died on June 29, 2009. When my mother told me, part of me felt relieved that he no longer had to suffer. That relief is a difficult thing to make sense of when you are a child who loves someone. Grief arrived in different forms afterward: the absence of a parent at ordinary moments, financial worries, a home learning to function differently, and the gradual realization that everybody else was still growing up with stories I would never have with him.

I had decided I wanted to speak at his funeral. I remember how important that was to me, even though it was an enormous thing to ask of a ten-year-old. I wanted to do something for him with the small voice I had. When I looked out at the people gathered there, it struck me that he had touched hundreds of lives simply by taking the lives around him seriously. He had never needed to become famous to do work that lasted. He had done it through his students, his family, and the people who knew they could turn to him.

One of the lines I have carried from a tribute to my dad was his answer when someone asked how he would live if he knew today were his last day: 'I wouldn’t live it any differently.' I have thought about that for most of my life. I am not sure I could give that answer yet. I am ambitious, and I have an almost comically long list of things I would love to make. But I want to be able to say that I took care of the people in front of me while trying. The lesson I took from losing him was an urgency to participate in life, to say yes to difficult things, and to leave something useful behind.

Vernal showed up for my family. People brought help, offered kindness, and kept caring long after the funeral. That matters just as much to this story as the loss itself. It gave me a living example of a community doing what people say they wish communities would do. I have been interested ever since in how to build more of that feeling into the places and systems we share.

sections.title: I started by trying to make people feel seen
sections.subtitle: Teenage years · Uintah High School
sections.preview: There is a slightly ridiculous amount of satisfaction in having a poster waiting for somebody when they come out of class. The whole thing could be made of inexpensive paper and tape. You still had to notice the person, learn enough to say something worthwhile, make it, and get it onto the wall without ruining the surprise. That was the part I loved. Not the paper. The moment someone realized other people had been paying attention.
sections.expanded:
My parents and the town had taught me that small acts of attention have weight. When I looked around school, I saw how unevenly that attention was distributed. The same names appeared on awards and banners. Plenty of other students were doing extraordinary things quietly, including just getting themselves through a difficult week. I wanted there to be room for them on the walls too.

I ran for an arts-focused student-government position even though I was hardly an accomplished visual artist. I liked the practical freedom of the role. Nobody needed another person to announce that the hallway was gray. I could arrive early, stay after classes, bring supplies in on the weekend, and make it look different. The building started becoming a kind of giant canvas, although quite a lot of it still remained concrete.

I spent time meeting with school counselors and administrators, trying to understand the students and parts of the school that did not get much attention. When I heard about somebody who had been generous or had shown a kind of resilience nobody was celebrating, I would make a poster for them. I might barely know the person. I would put it up while they were in class so they could walk out and discover somebody had seen them. The students would sometimes ask whether they could keep the posters. I remember that with more affection than I remember a lot of official student-government work.

School leadership also taught me how much effort hides behind a good experience. Somebody has to get approval, bring a ladder, move furniture, call the people responsible for facilities, arrange for cleanup, and work out what will happen when a thousand students arrive the next morning. The idea might be exciting, but the execution is where people find out whether they can trust you.

I was not always perfectly suited to the institution around me. I often felt different from my hometown in interests and personality, and later in values. That never made me want to give up on the place. I knew what it had done for my family. Caring about a community and wanting it to change have always felt compatible to me. In some ways, that is why I kept asking for permission to try things. I loved the school enough to think it could be better.

Years before anyone would call me a product manager, I was looking for friction, listening to the people who experienced it, and testing interventions that might change how a place felt. A handmade poster is a tiny thing. To the person who kept it, it clearly wasn't.

sections.title: I learned to build an experience before I knew the word product
sections.subtitle: Teenage years · Theater, school productions, and design
sections.preview: Theater is also a great place to discover that you can care very deeply about something while looking completely ridiculous doing it. You rehearse the same sequence until you're sick of hearing the music. Then someone gets a costume wrong, a prop disappears, or a microphone decides to stop participating. You fix it because the audience didn't come to watch you complain about the microphone. They came for a show.
sections.expanded:
I have loved theater for as long as I can remember. There is something extraordinary about gathering a room full of people and convincing them to temporarily accept another world. A stage can become the ocean, a car can fly, and somebody you know from math class can suddenly be a prince. Everyone in the audience understands the trick and somehow agrees to believe it anyway.

When I began performing in high school, I grew interested in the parts of theater that happened offstage. The director had enough to worry about just putting on a production. Marketing could easily become an afterthought. I took an interest in it because I was convinced the experience should begin before anyone bought a ticket. I wanted people walking through school to feel the show approaching.

For The Little Mermaid, I helped create enormous installations throughout the building and outside it. There were seaweed curtains, banners, pieces suspended overhead, and promotional materials designed to be impossible to ignore. They had to be sturdy, movable, easy to store, and safe in a school where ordinary classes were still happening. I learned to care about the spectacular vision and the humble logistical detail at the same time. Those are rarely separate problems.

The program reached attendance levels it had not seen before. I would never claim a single student caused all of that. Great casts, teachers, technical teams, and an entire community made the productions work. My contribution was to treat the audience's experience as something larger than the two hours they spent in a seat. By senior year our school mounted a production of Chitty Chitty Bang Bang costing roughly $55,000, with a car that genuinely flew above a stage in Vernal, Utah. I still think that is a remarkable sentence.

I was recognized among the top high-school actors in the state twice. I enjoyed being onstage and loved the camaraderie that came with working hard toward an opening night. But what continued to fascinate me was how many distinct crafts had to agree with one another for the audience to experience one coherent experience. A stage manager, costume designer, actor, technician, and publicist could all have different concerns and still be working toward the same moment.

Theater made me sensitive to pacing, emotion, and the effect of small choices. A line delivered a second too quickly may not land. A badly placed prop can make the audience worry about the prop instead of the scene. The whole experience can fail at the edges even when the center is wonderful. I carry that way of seeing into software. It is one reason I care about the button somebody sees when they are confused, the explanation that arrives at the right time, and the quiet details that make a new product feel like somebody thought it through.

sections.title: At sixteen I called city hall
sections.subtitle: Ages fifteen to twenty-one · City, county, and state government
sections.preview: I had absolutely no special qualification for calling the city manager. I was a teenager who wanted to learn how government worked. Fortunately, it turned out that asking was an option. That seems obvious now. At the time, it was a rather thrilling discovery: people who do interesting work are sometimes willing to let you see it, especially when you are prepared to be useful.
sections.expanded:
There were budgets and public works decisions and problems that could not be fixed simply by saying someone should fix them. I started to appreciate the unglamorous machinery that lets a community function. Later, working around county tourism and events, I helped coordinate parades, public performances, and unusual school experiences. We found a way to hold a dance at an airport. For a homecoming event, I coordinated with a hospital so a Life Flight helicopter could deliver the football. It was the kind of work where somebody has a wild idea and another person has to call the people who own the helicopter.

Government interested me because the systems affect real people, even when those people cannot see the system. I still carry that instinct into software: understand the constraints, find the person who knows the part you do not, and make the experience easier on the person waiting at the other end.

That early interest in public systems never entirely disappeared. I found the work of government compelling because it was full of invisible dependencies. Somebody could propose a better park or road, but that idea had to travel through budgets, property, departments, legal requirements, and the public's very different opinions about what mattered. I began to understand why a good-sounding suggestion can take so long to become real.

My later work with county tourism and community events gave that lesson a more playful side. I liked asking people to cooperate on a strange idea. A hospital helicopter delivering a football for homecoming sounds absurd until somebody has made the calls, worked out the rules, arranged the logistics, and gotten approval. A dance at an airport becomes possible in much the same way. The magic usually depends on an astonishing number of ordinary conversations.

Washington stayed in my imagination through all of it. The monuments were impressive, but the thought that interested me was that people had once argued about whether these things should exist at all. Somebody had imagined a building or an institution, built a coalition, and found the means to create it. I was growing up in a small town and beginning to see how much bigger a person's working world could become while still feeling responsible for the place they started.

sections.title: The impossible arch over the road
sections.subtitle: 2016 to 2023 · The Uintah Resilience Arch
sections.preview: The whole thing started with pieces of an old arch sitting in a yard. Not exactly the opening scene of a glamorous construction project. I saw them and thought about how much I wanted the entrance to my high school to feel like an arrival. I was still in school when I started drawing. I didn't understand what engineers would need, what steel would cost, or why getting something over a public roadway was a very different proposition from making a spectacular hallway display. In retrospect, the principal's condition that I find the money was a remarkably effective way to find out whether I meant it.
sections.expanded:
I first encountered the remains of the old arch in a yard, where they had ended up after the road was widened. We wanted the tradition back, but the original structure did not fit the new road. I started sketching a replacement in debate class, drawing something larger and more permanent, with lighting and lettering that could survive future changes. I presented the concept to school leadership and got the kind of answer that should probably come with a warning: find the money and you can make it happen.

At first, I underestimated the cost. I began with a fundraising target that seemed enormous to a high-school student and kept discovering the world of steel fabrication, engineering, transportation, concrete, excavation, electrical work, and insurance. I made phone calls to regional businesses and people who had no reason to trust that an eighteen-year-old could coordinate a project of this size. Some were generous immediately. Others had been approached about community projects that never reached completion. Someone told me that nothing like this ever gets done, and I found that sentence extremely irritating. It also became a useful warning about what I would have to prove.

I did not weld the steel or sign the engineering drawings. Skilled people did that work. I organized the people, fundraising, approvals, and persistence required for their work to meet in one physical place. The project raised about $100,000. It was my first long lesson in how much of leadership consists of making it possible for other people to do what they are excellent at.

Along the way I became uncomfortable with the idea of building a monument to the school while some of its most remarkable students went unrecognized. I knew students managing circumstances no application could capture: unstable housing, family responsibilities, money problems, and difficult homes. I founded a resilience scholarship to recognize that kind of effort. Seven scholarships had been awarded when I wrote my original career story. I want that part of the project to keep living long after people forget who made the first phone call.

I named it the Resilience Arch. The name belongs as much to the town that looked after my family as it does to the students walking beneath it.

When the project stalled during a two-year period I spent working overseas, I had to confront the difference between having started something and having made it resilient enough to continue without me. The transition between school leaders did not simplify anything. I came back and resumed calling donors, contractors, engineers, and administrators. There were moments when I felt embarrassed to make another request from people who had already given so much. The easiest way out would have been to call the undertaking a good learning experience and quietly let it go.

I could not do that because the promise had become communal. People had donated money, materials, labor, and trust. One person supplied a piece of fabrication expertise. Another found transportation. Another worked out the electrical or concrete requirements. It was never my job to pretend I could do those things personally. I needed to make their contributions fit together and keep the next person moving even when another part of the project was delayed.

By the time the structure was finished, it stood about twenty-five feet high and spanned sixty-three feet. Roughly $100,000 in money, labor, and donated materials had supported the work. In one of the earlier versions of the story, I counted the turnover it had survived: three principals, two school boards, and two superintendents. The finished arch was so much more durable than my original drawing because knowledgeable people had improved the idea. It is still one of my favorite illustrations of what a leader can accomplish by persuading other people that a project is worth their craft.

When I drive beneath it, I see the businesses and townspeople who made it possible. I also see my younger self, who was annoyingly willing to make one more phone call. I hope students see that somebody their age can begin a thing that feels far too large for them. That is worth putting over a road.

sections.title: Two years of pro bono work and a system nobody wanted to use
sections.subtitle: 2017 to 2019 · Birmingham, England
sections.preview: England gave me two experiences that don't sound as though they belong together. I spent an extraordinary amount of time talking with strangers who didn't want to talk with me. And I spent an extraordinary amount of time looking at spreadsheets. Both turned out to be useful. The first taught me that someone saying no isn't an invitation to argue with them. The second taught me that a badly designed reporting process can make hundreds of people's jobs more irritating than necessary.
sections.expanded:
When people see two years of volunteer work on a résumé, they can reasonably wonder what that looked like day to day. It was intensive. The hours were long, the schedule was structured, and a great deal of the work involved people who did not have any particular reason to listen to us. I became comfortable introducing myself to strangers, getting a polite no, and trying again without taking it personally. Being persistent while respecting somebody else's lack of interest is a skill I still value.

Over time, I was given broader operational responsibilities that included helping leaders coordinate teams across a geographically dispersed organization. There were hundreds of volunteers, twenty or more regions, financial procedures to follow, and constant changes in who was doing what. Much of the information was collected through slow reporting processes and then reentered or compiled by hand. The administrative effort was stealing time from the people who needed to act on the information.

I had never studied computer science and did not arrive with a programmer's confidence. We had limited tablets and spreadsheets, which turned out to be enough to start. I learned formulas, structured the inputs, designed dashboards and reporting flows, and kept testing where the system would fail when someone used it in an unexpected way. I eventually built three internal reporting and analytics tools. My later résumé recorded a reduction from roughly two days of administrative reporting to about three hours. The original story remembered a little over a day becoming around two hours for a particular weekly reporting process. Either way, the change was meaningful to the people who were doing the work.

There were other responsibilities: helping train hundreds of volunteers, communicating across regions, reconciling operating expenses, and trying to give leaders useful information rather than another pile of submissions. A system can be logically elegant and still be useless if the people who need it do not adopt it. That was one of the first times I had to think seriously about teaching people a new workflow and making it better enough that they would stop doing the old one.

I enjoyed the sense that I was being given problems slightly larger than my training. It was frustrating and exhilarating in equal measure. I had to learn what the user needed, ask the people affected, account for edge cases, and work inside real constraints. I did not know those were the kinds of tasks product managers did. I only knew I loved the feeling of giving someone a tool that returned time to their day.

The work also taught me that the most useful leader in a complicated environment is not necessarily the person who speaks most confidently. Often it is the person who notices where communication breaks down, asks one more question, and gets everyone working from the same information. That stayed with me when I returned to the United States and started trying to figure out what sort of career could combine so many interests.

sections.title: Coming home to a world that suddenly changed
sections.subtitle: 2019 to 2021 · Utah, government, and research
sections.preview: I came back from England with a lot of experience and very little idea how to explain it. I'd learned to coordinate people, solve awkward operational problems, and work under pressure. But none of it came packaged as the usual college internship. So I did what I often do when I don't know exactly where I'm going: I started asking questions, applied for opportunities that sounded interesting, and tried to be useful once I got there. I found myself around government, research, and events, which, admittedly, did not make choosing a major easier.
sections.expanded:
I came home to a life that had changed while I was away. Friends were further along in school. I had two years of demanding experience behind me and none of the conventional signals that made it easy to explain. I wanted to learn a great deal, perhaps more than I could reasonably fit into a degree. Politics and public service still interested me, and I was curious about research, business, and the social systems that could make a person’s life better or worse.

I had been encouraged years earlier to follow up about a state-government opportunity after returning. I did. It led to work in and around the Utah Governor’s Office. I got to see how constituent correspondence and briefings turn into the everyday work of a public institution. It is easy to imagine government as speeches and legislation. A surprising amount is responding responsibly to an ordinary person who needs help and does not know which office owns the problem.

When the pandemic began, I worked with the Governor’s Office of Economic Development as businesses struggled with sudden restrictions, uncertainty, and complicated assistance requirements. My later career notes recorded advising roughly 950 businesses on federal grant guidelines. I remember the pressure of that time more than any one statistic. People were trying to understand what they qualified for, what they needed to submit, and whether the help would arrive before their business failed. An unclear form could mean hours lost by someone who did not have hours to spare.

I was also involved in research at BYU’s Public Ethics Lab, where our work drew on interviews with local-government participants and data that required careful analysis. I learned to sit with an untidy collection of evidence and ask what conclusion it supported. I liked research because it asked for curiosity and discipline in equal measure. The findings were only useful if we could explain them clearly to the people who might use them.

Around the same period I worked with TEDxSaltLakeCity, coordinating volunteers and helping with the production side of an event built around ideas. That felt familiar. I could watch talented people who thought about very different things come together to make a shared experience for an audience. I loved the practical detail of that work, from getting people into the right room to making sure the program would run.

I began to see a pattern in the things I liked. I wanted to understand systems well enough to change them. I also wanted to be near the people living with the consequences. In government, research, and events, that meant listening to people and figuring out how information became action. Those experiences were beginning to point me toward a field I had barely heard named.

sections.title: I finally discovered what product management was
sections.subtitle: 2020 to 2022 · College and entrepreneurship
sections.preview: For a long time I thought having so many interests was a problem I ought to fix. I loved government, theater, design, business, research, technology, and the actual act of organizing people around an idea. That is an inconvenient collection of things to fit under one academic department. Then I encountered product management and discovered there was apparently a job where people were expected to care about several of those things at once. I was relieved. I was also very interested in finding out whether the job was actually as good as it sounded.
sections.expanded:
To get into the program I worked through a short hackathon with people who knew things I did not. My contribution was to get out of the room, talk to users, understand what they needed, and bring that evidence back to the designer and engineer. The same pattern continued once we formed BackLocal, a business software project, and began working toward a revenue-generating launch.

I led product strategy, research, branding, prioritization, and a team that included five engineers and two UX designers. Across interviews and surveys we gathered input from more than 370 prospective users, according to my later career records. We shipped a B2B subscription product that generated revenue during the program. I learned how quickly an ambitious roadmap has to meet the realities of engineering capacity, customer interest, and a group of people with different motivations.

I was also working on research and community projects, including the BYU Public Ethics Lab and TEDxSaltLakeCity. What kept me interested was the same thing across all of it. There was a complicated human problem, a group of people who knew different pieces, and an opportunity to build something they could use.

I remember the relief of discovering that I was allowed to be interested in several disciplines at once. I had spent years feeling torn between the arts, government, business, and technology, as though a responsible person was supposed to choose only one. Product work rewarded the ability to understand how the pieces affected each other. A customer might be asking for something design could solve, but the answer might depend on the database, a contract, a business model, or a policy decision. That complexity felt exciting instead of discouraging.

Getting into Sandbox was its own lesson in taking initiative. The entrance process included a rapid build with a small group: a designer, an engineer, somebody with a psychology background, and me. We did not have days to conduct beautiful research. I went into stores, asked people questions, called potential users, and brought back information we could turn into decisions. We had roughly thirty-six hours. By the end, I knew that getting out of the room to understand the user was the part I wanted to do over and over.

I also learned that a good idea is allowed to change when the evidence changes. I was drawn to entrepreneurship because it combines optimism with an uncomfortable requirement to be wrong in public. You can be convinced the world needs something, spend weeks designing it, and discover the customer has never had the problem you thought they had. That is painful and useful. I would rather find out before the team has built an entire monument to a misunderstanding.

The coursework gave me concepts for things I had already encountered in the wild: discovery, priorities, value propositions, workflows, economics, adoption, and the compromises required by limited resources. As much as I enjoyed understanding the theory, I wanted a team and an actual product. Sandbox offered the possibility of learning while building something real.

sections.title: BackLocal made the classroom feel very small
sections.subtitle: 2021 to 2022 · Sandbox at BYU
sections.preview: The difference between presenting a startup idea in class and asking a stranger to pay for it is enormous. In class, people are encouraged to be interested. A real customer has other things to do. They don't have to admire your slide deck, forgive the confusing onboarding, or use a product because you stayed awake finishing it. BackLocal was where that distinction stopped being theoretical for me.
sections.expanded:
Sandbox was structured around building a real company. We had faculty and industry mentors, but the product could still fail. Prospective customers could tell us they had no interest. Team members could miss commitments. Engineers could spend all week on a technically sound approach and still discover that it did not answer the user's most important question. There was no way to hide all of that behind a grade.

I became Head of Product at BackLocal and ended up involved in far more than a typical classroom project would require. I worked on product strategy, customer discovery, design direction, brand and positioning, priorities, recruitment, and difficult conversations with teammates. My later résumé records research with more than 370 prospective users across interviews and surveys, followed by a revenue-generating B2B subscription launch. I was proud that something we designed became something somebody would pay for.

Our technical capacity was a lesson in itself. A team can have an engineering role filled and still be early in developing the skills required by its ambitions. We recruited additional help and I coordinated work involving five engineers and two UX designers, alongside other contributors. Some people were there because they dreamed about founding companies. Others had different priorities. I learned that the job of keeping the team moving requires understanding what each person can deliver and being willing to have uncomfortable conversations before an avoidable problem becomes everybody's emergency.

We also learned quickly that good-looking software is only the beginning of a business. If an onboarding flow is clumsy, people leave. If the offer is confusing, sales conversations stall. If a feature takes four times longer than expected, the rest of the roadmap changes. The product manager cannot solve those problems by announcing a deadline. Somebody has to understand what is happening and coordinate a realistic way forward.

That was where my earlier experiences began coming together. The interviews reminded me of asking students how school felt. The coordination reminded me of the arch. The visual decisions reminded me of theater. The financial and operational tradeoffs reminded me of government. All of those experiences were suddenly useful in a field I had only recently discovered.

I did not leave Sandbox with a permanent company. I left with something I consider more valuable for that stage of my career: a real understanding of how incomplete information, different personalities, and limited time shape a product. It also made me comfortable owning work before I felt completely qualified to own it. That habit would matter a great deal at Crew.

sections.title: Theater became my model for working with a team
sections.subtitle: 2021 to 2024 · Young Ambassadors and professional theater
sections.preview: There were days when my life seemed to be split between spreadsheets and choreography. I'd spend time thinking about customers, engineering priorities, or a business model, and then go rehearse a song until every muscle in my body remembered it. I liked both. I also learned that a cast of talented performers and a team of talented engineers can be similarly stubborn, generous, tired, funny, and dependent on one another.
sections.expanded:
A production brings together specialists who see completely different parts of the same experience. The lighting designer knows things the performer cannot know. The costume designer has constraints the choreographer may not have considered. The director has to make room for those crafts while protecting the audience’s experience. The best productions I have been part of were demanding, collaborative, and generous with credit.

I see product the same way. A PM needs a clear sense of the audience and the problem, enough technical understanding to recognize a hard constraint, and the humility to know when the engineer or designer should lead the decision. I enjoy being the person who keeps the whole production in view. It is much less interesting to win an argument than to help the team make the thing better.

Performing also gives you immediate feedback. The joke either reaches the room or it does not. You can rehearse a moment for weeks and still discover that the audience understands something differently. Customer research feels familiar for that reason. The audience gets a vote in what the experience means, whether the people making it planned for that or not.

Young Ambassadors demanded a kind of discipline that people who only see a performance can easily miss. Rehearsals required repeating an eight-count until everybody was in the right place, learning changes quickly, and making dozens of individual choices fit into a single show. I was one of the people arriving from outside the usual academic track. At times that made me feel like I had to prove I deserved to be there. It also made me work harder to understand the craft and respect the people who had spent years studying it.

Touring raised the stakes. Travel problems, unfamiliar venues, technical constraints, and exhaustion did not excuse a sloppy performance. You learned to give the audience what they had come for while taking care of the people beside you. I like that combination of high standards and mutual dependence. Nobody in a great production is so talented that they can replace everybody else.

When I later performed in Elf at Hale Centre Theatre, I was also working in a demanding professional environment during the day. For the run of the show, there was not much space for anything else. I did it because the theater mattered to me and because I did not want my creative life to become an old story I told people about high school. I still want to perform. I still write and think in scenes. The part of me that loves spectacle has never left.

At work, I think of myself less as the star of a show and more as the person responsible for making the whole show possible. A strong engineer should be able to tell me that a proposed behavior is technically fragile. A great designer should be able to push me toward something more intuitive than the first requirement described. The person talking to customers may know something none of us have heard. What matters is that the team's different specialties become coherent for the person on the receiving end.

Theater is also a wonderfully immediate form of user research. You can hear whether an audience laughs. You can feel confusion in a room. If a scene goes long, the audience does not care how many hours you rehearsed it. They experience the result. I have carried that humility through my product career. People using software are not obligated to appreciate our effort. We have to make an experience that serves them.

sections.title: At Divvy, I learned how easily data can mislead
sections.subtitle: June to September 2022 · Divvy, now BILL
sections.preview: An analytics dashboard can look wonderfully authoritative while telling you something completely wrong. That's what made Divvy such a good education. Nobody was trying to mislead anyone. The company had grown, products had changed, and the instrumentation wasn't consistently keeping up. A beautiful chart is not much help when different teams mean different things by the same event. I was fascinated by how much important decision-making rested on those small, invisible definitions.
sections.expanded:
I partnered with eight product managers, worked on the underlying event taxonomy and interface tagging, and helped bring analytics accuracy to 93%. I trained thirteen cross-functional teams to use a more consistent system. Once the data became more dependable, we could look at funnels, adoption, and the points where users abandoned a flow instead of relying only on what somebody remembered from a meeting.

The experience sharpened a conviction I still have. Good instinct is useful. I want mine to be fed good information. Behavioral data shows where people struggle; interviews often tell you why. Both need careful interpretation, especially when the easiest number to measure is nowhere near the outcome that matters.

I liked that work and expected to keep growing in it. Then a window opened that I had been thinking about since my first visit to Washington.

What interested me about Divvy was the level of complexity behind an apparently simple product metric. Somebody could ask how many people had completed a flow, and the answer depended on whether the same action had been tracked consistently across platforms, what happened after a user reopened the app, and whether the event represented the thing a product manager thought it represented. When teams disagree about definitions, the disagreement can hide inside the dashboard for a surprisingly long time.

I worked as an analytics partner to eight product managers and spent time looking at the experience from their perspective. They needed to understand where people got stuck, where steps were redundant, which features customers used, and where an assumption might be worth testing. I partnered with engineers on tagging and data quality and helped thirteen teams work with more consistent definitions. Improving the instrumentation was unglamorous, but it made the next conversation about the customer considerably better.

That work also taught me to be cautious about treating a metric as an explanation. A funnel can tell you where a user leaves. It cannot automatically tell you whether the person was confused, distracted, wary of sharing information, or simply uninterested in the product. I began to value the pairing of quantitative evidence with the careful observation I had learned in theater and customer interviews.

I liked the role very much. I was learning inside a mature product organization with strong colleagues and a clearer view of what excellent product practice looked like at scale. Leaving after a short period was not part of the plan. Then I had the chance to take a position in Washington that I had wanted for years. It was an awkward choice for the cleanest possible résumé, and an easy choice for the person I was trying to become.

sections.title: I finally went to work in Washington
sections.subtitle: September to December 2022 · Washington, D.C.
sections.preview: I had been imagining a job in Washington since I first visited as a teenager. So when the opportunity came to work in a Senate office, I took it seriously. The interesting part wasn't the proximity to famous people. It was realizing how quickly a lofty political question could turn into an actual person waiting for an answer, or an extremely technical issue that couldn't be understood by reading the headline.
sections.expanded:
I helped with constituent services and saw how often a complaint that sounded political was rooted in something immediate: a bill someone could not pay, uncertainty about a family member, or the fear that nobody was listening. My job was to pay attention to what the person needed beneath the wording of the request.

I also worked on policy research, including nuclear licensing. I was an intern without a nuclear-engineering background. I went through hundreds of pages of technical material and turned what I had learned into a short brief for staff. My later résumé records roughly 500 pages condensed into two. The difficult part was being clear about what I understood, what remained uncertain, and whose expertise we needed.

The internship confirmed my affection for the city and taught me a useful discipline for product: enter an unfamiliar domain with curiosity, do the reading, ask good questions, and avoid pretending you already know it all. I was happy to learn that I could be useful quickly. I was just as happy to return to building products afterward.

I had been carrying a picture of Washington in my head since that first student trip. Returning to work there was thrilling, even though much of the daily work bore little resemblance to the grandeur outside the office windows. There were constituent concerns to process, questions requiring careful routing, deadlines, schedules, staff meetings, and a great deal of reading. I loved the contrast. The city is full of monuments to enormous ideas, and inside its institutions people still have to do the ordinary work that makes a decision possible.

One part of my job was listening to constituents and trying to understand the need behind what they were telling us. A person might call about a policy and sound angry, but the anxiety underneath could be about money, safety, fairness, or whether someone in power had heard them at all. I had encountered the same pattern in schools and local government. Listening closely meant refusing to stop at the loudest sentence.

At one point I was assigned research involving nuclear policy and licensing. I was a young intern and had no business pretending to be a nuclear engineer. The material was dense, technical, and full of rules with real-world consequences. My later résumé described reducing hundreds of pages of material into a two-page brief that could support appropriations work. I had to understand the structure of the issue, recognize the limits of my expertise, and produce something a more experienced person could use. That is an important distinction. Being useful in an unfamiliar field requires knowing enough to locate the experts and ask a better question.

For all I enjoyed Washington, the experience also clarified that I did not want to spend my entire career in government. I wanted to create things more directly and work with teams who could test a new idea against what happened when people used it. That realization made the next invitation especially compelling.

I was still technically finishing my education. My career already had more than one detour in it. I decided to judge the opportunity by what I would learn and the work I could contribute rather than by how neatly the dates lined up on a résumé.

sections.title: At Crew, I got to help write the show
sections.subtitle: December 2022 to April 2024 · Willow, then Crew Finance
sections.preview: Crew is the job I still have the hardest time summarizing. 'Product manager' is technically useful, but it doesn't explain how often I was learning something on Tuesday because a decision needed to be made on Wednesday. There were very few of us. We were trying to build financial products for families, and every new ambition seemed to reveal another vendor, contract, regulation, or design question. I loved the scope. I also learned, rather painfully at times, that loving the scope doesn't make it smaller.
sections.expanded:
The original concept, then called Willow, involved a premium family-oriented credit product. We explored rewards, card materials, and the economics underneath the offer. The required financing structure did not materialize as planned, so the company shifted toward debit. A pivot like that reaches into almost everything. The customer promise changes, the economics change, and the design decisions you were proud of last month may need to be reconsidered.

I became a Senior Product Manager, working directly with the founder, CTO, designer, engineers, and outside partners. In a company that small, a title did very little to limit the size of the work. I helped lead the card program and the customer-facing experience around it. I could spend the morning on risk or identity verification, the afternoon with a card manufacturer, and the evening revising onboarding language because a parent did not understand what would happen next.

I learned more about payments infrastructure in those months than I could have learned by watching a stack of webinars. You build a debit program by understanding what happens when the customer taps a card, who may authorize the transaction, where the funds sit, who handles disputes, and how several organizations are supposed to work together under rules that do not care about your sprint schedule.

The company began under the name Willow before becoming Crew. The early idea involved helping families manage money with a more thoughtful set of tools, and we investigated a premium credit product before moving toward a debit-centered experience. That transition sounded simple if you looked only at the card's shape. It changed the economics, the financing assumptions, the partner relationships, the risk model, and the product we could reasonably promise. It was my first close view of how thoroughly a business constraint can rewrite a roadmap.

I joined as a founding employee, never a cofounder, and worked directly with the CEO, CTO, lead designer, engineers, and partners. In roughly three months the startup raised around $2.5 million and grew from the early concept into a small team that was trying to launch something regulated. My scope widened rapidly because there were gaps between the functions a financial product needed and the number of people we could afford to hire. I liked that responsibility, even when it meant spending the evening learning an entirely unfamiliar part of the industry.

In a larger company, there might be separate owners for card issuance, supplier relationships, onboarding, activation, research, acquisition, packaging, and portions of the brand experience. At Crew those things affected each other every day. A change to a card material could change the fulfillment cost. A compliance requirement could alter the signup flow. A new onboarding idea could require work from a processor or our issuing bank before the team could make a responsible promise to users.

I also learned to take seriously the work that a person cannot see. The more polished the eventual product looked, the more somebody had probably spent time resolving the ugly dependencies underneath. I was proud to be one of the people who knew which doors had to be opened, what decisions were still uncertain, and when the team needed to slow down because a feature depended on a commitment we did not yet have.

I wanted to make a family banking experience that felt credible to adults and welcoming to children. Those audiences arrive with very different kinds of fear. A parent wants to know their money is safe and their child can learn to handle it. A kid wants to feel trusted and capable. Every choice, from the account structure to the illustrations, had to respect those motivations. That combination made Crew a wonderful place to learn product: the work was complex enough to be humbling and human enough to be worth caring about.

sections.title: There is an entire financial system behind a debit card
sections.subtitle: 2023 to 2024 · Crew product and banking infrastructure
sections.preview: Before working at Crew, I understood a debit card mostly from the side of the person who takes it out of a wallet. Afterward, I couldn't see one without imagining the network, the bank, the processor, the card manufacturer, the personalization process, the support arrangements, and the compliance decisions. That knowledge has probably made me a less interesting person to stand behind in a checkout line. A card is a wonderfully simple object supported by a surprisingly complicated institution.
sections.expanded:
If you have never worked on a card program, it is easy to assume that designing a debit card is mostly a graphic design assignment. You choose the color and the logo, find a manufacturer, and wait for a box to arrive. I had some version of that assumption before I started. The chain is much longer and more expensive in practice.

We had to understand the relationship between the consumer-facing fintech and the legal issuing bank, the Mastercard network, the processor, and the various vendors involved in creating and delivering a physical card. At Crew, Bangor Savings Bank was the issuing bank. I learned about BIN or IIN ranges, card product configuration, transaction authorization, secure personalization, fulfillment, and the difference between an appealing interface and the institution that enforces the underlying rule. I was coordinating product and supplier work with the people responsible for legal, compliance, engineering, and banking decisions. I was never pretending to be the lawyer or the bank.

We researched materials and manufacturing methods. A premium metal card sounds like a product feature until you have to account for the antenna, chip, weight, personalization method, minimum production order, and every step that follows. A beautiful sample can fail the economics of the customer you intend to serve. A low unit price can become a high total price once storage, setup, fulfillment, delivery, and unsuccessful shipments are included. Some of my favorite product decisions were decisions to let go of something visually exciting because another option was better for the business and the user.

The original Willow concepts explored credit, premium rewards, and early-payment incentives. A credit card requires financing that a debit card does not, and a rewards promise has to be supported by the actual revenue and risk structure. We modeled assumptions about purchase frequency, interchange, deposits, and transaction fees. I learned that a few basis points or a few cents per transaction can change an entire financial projection when the numbers scale. The most valuable spreadsheet is often the one that makes an attractive idea visibly unsustainable before it becomes a contractual obligation.

Families introduced another set of requirements. Parents needed to understand who could own an account, what permissions could apply to children, how funds moved, and which controls would be enforced by the actual transaction system rather than merely displayed in the app. Identity verification, bank-linking capabilities, age-sensitive data, account ownership, and KYC obligations all shaped the experience. We had to consider how a parent could give a child more independence without accidentally making the interface promise a control the underlying infrastructure could not enforce.

The card also had to get into somebody's hand. That meant card artwork, manufacturing specifications, personalization, packaging, shipping, activation, returns, and the dependencies that connect them. We needed to understand what happened when an address was wrong, a card had not arrived, a linked bank could not support a particular verification method, or a transaction appeared pending even after approval. Those are not edge cases to the customer standing in front of a checkout terminal. They are the product working or failing at the exact moment it matters.

I came away from Crew able to work more comfortably across technical and nontechnical groups. I could speak with engineers about what needed to be represented in an application, with a supplier about what could physically be manufactured, and with the founder about how the decisions affected our economics. I had developed technical fluency through responsibility. Knowing enough to connect the specialists was an essential part of my job.

sections.title: I drew the Crew brand on an iPad
sections.subtitle: 2023 to 2024 · Crew brand and experience
sections.preview: I was drawing on my iPad when the brand work started taking shape. That's a slightly embarrassing beginning for a serious financial-services identity, but it's true. We needed something a parent could trust and a child would actually want to use. I didn't have an agency sitting in the next room ready to solve that problem. I had an idea, a screen, a designer to collaborate with, and a lot to learn about where a visual system meets a physical product.
sections.expanded:
Family banking is a delicate thing to design. Parents need to trust the place holding their money. Kids need to feel that the product belongs to them too. A family product can slip into looking childish, and a traditional bank can feel cold enough to scare off the very people it wants to reach. I was absorbed by the line between reassuring and interesting.

Because we were building before we had a mature analytics stack, I went out and talked to people. I did customer interviews in ordinary places, including malls, watched where people hesitated in onboarding, and looked for the questions they asked without prompting. Sometimes the most useful information was a few seconds of confusion. It could tell us that the problem was trust or that a person did not understand how a card would get to their house.

I carried that information back into decisions about onboarding and positioning. In my later work records, our tests are credited with cutting onboarding time by about half, alongside improvements in engagement and return behavior. I remain careful about what any one metric proves. The human reaction behind the number is the part I remember most clearly.

I also learned how to argue for a recommendation without treating a disagreement as an insult. Founders have decision rights. Product managers have a responsibility to bring evidence and judgment into the room. You can do that well and still make a decision different from the one you preferred.

I learned a great deal about visual identity by trying to make one that could survive the ordinary demands of a growing product. An illustration is lovely until you need a version for a tiny mobile screen, another for an email, and another for a card carrier. A color can feel distinctive on a computer and wrong on a manufactured surface. A tone of voice that makes a child smile may make a parent wonder whether this company is serious about their money. The brand had to be flexible enough to accommodate all of that without becoming a collection of unrelated clever ideas.

My historical work records describe producing fifty-two illustrations for Crew. The number is less important to me than the logic of a reusable system. We needed different images for onboarding, family situations, product explanations, and campaigns, but we could not invent an entirely new style every time someone needed another screen. I worked to make the materials feel related and to give the team assets it could keep using after the first launch.

I paid attention to what the customer touched outside the app. The card, the paper around it, the packaging, the first instructions, and the unboxing all told a story about what the company valued. An overdesigned mailer might impress somebody for five seconds while quietly adding expense to every future customer. We explored packaging choices with an eye toward both perceived quality and unit economics. Some of the cost savings were boring on paper and wonderful in aggregate.

The best part of that work was collaborating with the people who knew things I did not. Our UX designer could improve the structure of a screen I had proposed. Engineers could explain the technical or accessibility constraints I had missed. The founder could challenge whether an expensive visual idea served the customer. I could keep the throughline visible, moving between brand, cost, research, and product decisions.

One of my favorite things about design is that a person can feel how much thought went into a product without knowing the names of the decisions. They simply feel that it is coherent. I loved the possibility that a family would encounter Crew through an advertisement, use the signup experience, open the envelope, and receive a card that looked as though the same people had cared about the entire journey.

This was also the period when my creative life became increasingly integrated with my technical work. I had spent years designing experiences for audiences. At Crew, I was doing something similar with a completely different set of consequences. There was more regulation, more operational complexity, and considerably less room for the financial equivalent of a prop failing in the second act.

sections.title: When there was no dashboard, I went to the mall
sections.subtitle: 2023 to 2024 · Crew research, onboarding, and launch
sections.preview: One advantage of having almost no user data is that you cannot pretend the analytics have answered all your questions. You have to go find people. At Crew, that sometimes meant approaching families in ordinary places, including the mall, and asking about how they managed money. It is an efficient way to learn how little patience people have for a product explanation that makes perfect sense only to the person who wrote it.
sections.expanded:
Early-stage product research is humbling because the people you need may not be looking for what you are building. It is tempting to describe the idea beautifully, ask whether it sounds helpful, and count every polite smile as evidence. I had to become more careful than that. I tried to ask about how families already managed money, what made them anxious, what they trusted, and which changes to their lives they would be willing to make for a better product.

Going to malls and approaching strangers was an imperfect way to recruit people, but it got me outside the circle of people who knew the founders and wanted the company to succeed. I listened for the reasons people hesitated. One parent might worry about a child having a card at all. Another could be concerned about moving money to a company they had never heard of. Someone might like the family features and still have no interest in changing their primary checking account. Those objections forced us to distinguish the audience we wanted from the reason that audience might switch.

There were moments in the research that felt wonderfully small. Somebody would move through a flow and say it was quick without being prompted. Another would describe the interface as different from what they expected from a bank. That kind of response could validate a specific aspect of the experience. It still did not prove a person would fund an account or make us their primary bank. I learned to distinguish the small success from the much larger behavior we hoped it would lead to.

My product notes from that time talk about necessities, enhancements, and delighters. I wanted us to build the indispensable things well and then notice the places where an experience could exceed a person's expectation in a useful way. There is a difference between decorating a screen and removing a moment of uncertainty. One of them can look wonderful in a portfolio. The other can change how someone feels about trusting a product with their money.

I did not win every argument. Sometimes a founder's conviction remained stronger than the research I brought to the table. I learned how to present evidence without treating it as a weapon and how to execute a final decision that was not my own recommendation. Ownership of the research meant making sure the decision makers understood the evidence and the tradeoffs. The company still had legitimate decision rights, and I had to respect them.

We ran user testing and experiments as Crew moved toward launch. My résumé credits that work with cutting onboarding time by about half, increasing engagement around twenty percent, and improving return rates around sixty percent. Those numbers are from my career records and need the ordinary verification any published case study deserves, but the direction of the work is clear: remove friction, understand what people did next, and make it easier for a family to finish the job they had started.

Eventually the product moved from diagrams and partner calls into the hands of actual customers, beginning with friends and family and expanding beyond that circle. I remember how satisfying it felt to see the card, the app, the onboarding, and the operational systems work together. So much of the effort had been invisible. The launch made it visible in one ordinary action: somebody could use what we had built.

sections.title: The launch happened. The funding did not.
sections.subtitle: Spring 2024 · Crew and a difficult transition
sections.preview: I still remember how proud I felt that Crew launched. We'd crossed a ridiculous number of dependencies and made a real thing. Then we ran into a business reality that no amount of interface polish could fix: the financing we needed did not arrive on the timeline we needed it. The product had launched. The company was still vulnerable. Those two facts were true at the same time, and it was awful to discover how little the first protected us from the second.
sections.expanded:
I loved that job. The team was small enough that every person mattered to the daily work, and I had poured an extraordinary amount of attention into the product. On my last day I kept the meetings already on my calendar and made sure people knew where things stood. I would hesitate to tell somebody that is always the right response to a layoff. It was the response that made sense to me in that moment.

I have thought a lot about what that period taught me. A good team can be serious, talented, and hardworking while the company around it runs out of runway. Infrastructure, regulation, timing, and financing are part of the product environment too. Some of the ideas I had worked on survived in later versions of Crew, which was reassuring. I wanted the work to matter after I was gone.

The experience made me better at distinguishing the risks a team can manage from the risks it must acknowledge. It also reminded me how much I love working beside people who care about a hard problem.

I wish product stories were always as tidy as a case-study slide. There is a problem, the team makes a plan, a beautiful launch photograph appears, and the numbers move upward. Real companies have financing decisions, delays, partner dependencies, and a market that may not cooperate with the timing in the original plan. Crew taught me that the work can be excellent and the business can still become constrained in ways a product manager cannot solve through better prioritization alone.

The separation was painful because I felt attached to the entire team. I had helped create so much of the day-to-day operating structure, and I had spent months learning parts of the business that barely existed when I joined. On the day I was told the role was ending, I finished my scheduled work despite being told I could leave. I had meetings and an intern. There were things other people were waiting on. Looking back, I can see that no one should feel obligated to handle a layoff that way. It was how I responded in the moment because I wanted to leave the team with as little additional disruption as possible.

I went through a period of questioning what the experience meant. At the time, a short tenure and a layoff could look like a simple line on a résumé. I knew how many late nights, hard decisions, vendor calls, customer interviews, and technical compromises sat behind those dates. I also knew that explaining all of that to a stranger in a short application would be difficult.

Over time, I found comfort in seeing parts of the work continue after I had left. Products belong to teams and customers, and a good foundation should outlast any individual contributor. Some of the directions we had advocated for became important to later versions of the product. That gave me a better sense of what it means to contribute to something larger than myself.

I would do parts of the experience differently now. I would be more alert to financing constraints, ask harder questions about the assumptions behind a launch plan, and be more disciplined about the tradeoffs that matter most before a company runs short of time. Those are valuable lessons. I also left with more conviction that I liked complex product work and wanted to keep doing it with thoughtful, technically strong people.

sections.title: My education took its own route
sections.subtitle: 2023 to April 2025 · Transferring and finishing college
sections.preview: I don't have a particularly tidy education story. I worked, took opportunities, changed plans, and eventually had to make a decision about finishing my degree under circumstances that didn't fit the picture I'd once imagined. Transferring schools wasn't an exciting narrative twist. It was paperwork, lost credits, rearranged expectations, and the decision to finish what I'd started. I'm glad I did. I don't think the journey needs to be recast as a perfect master plan to count.
sections.expanded:
I could have tried to make the last stretch work on paper at my old school. It would have required me to live with a conflict I did not want to keep negotiating. Transferring came with trade-offs, including lost credits and online coursework while I worked. I made the choice and kept going.

The new degree path also brought more formal work in business analytics. That suited me. By then I had seen the difference between a polished strategy deck and evidence from a customer who had just struggled to use the product. Studying data alongside my work made the discipline more useful.

There is a version of this paragraph that could sound like an explanation for a gap. I would rather it be read as the record of a decision I am glad I made, followed by a commitment I kept.

There is a version of my educational history that is easy to summarize in one sentence: I started at BYU and graduated from UVU. The lived version was more complicated. I had spent years learning in settings that did not fit a standard class schedule. I was working at startups, trying to support myself, pursuing a demanding creative life, and realizing that some of the expectations around my original school no longer fit who I was becoming.

I made the decision to transfer with roughly a year of school remaining. The transfer cost me time. Courses and credits did not map neatly between the two programs, and I had to absorb the delay while continuing to work. The straightforward choice for a résumé might have been to remain where I was and quietly finish. It would have come with personal compromises I was no longer willing to make. I chose a path that let me complete my education while living more honestly.

UVU also gave me a stronger exposure to analytical work. The Business and Analysis program complemented the product experience I had acquired through building, research, and instrumentation. I liked that the degree could become useful in ways I could immediately apply rather than remain a credential kept apart from my day-to-day responsibilities.

I know recruiters may see the date and wonder why it took so long. It is a fair question. I had spent those years building companies, working in regulated financial products, serving in government, making theater, and taking a less direct educational path. I finished the degree in April 2025. I care deeply about that final fact because when I commit to an important piece of work, I want to see it through.

sections.title: I chose sales because I wanted to hear the word no
sections.subtitle: October 2024 to November 2025 · Utah Business and Deseret News
sections.preview: There is a peculiar confidence that comes from working on a product for years and believing you understand why somebody would pay for it. I wanted to test that confidence against reality. So I took a sales job. I wanted to sit across from the person who actually controlled the budget, hear what they cared about, and experience how quickly a compelling idea can become a less compelling invoice.
sections.expanded:
I worked across roughly 63 client relationships and a calendar involving 52 annual live events. I helped with package design, sales, activation, and renewal conversations. I inherited no established personal book of prospects and had to build relationships in a market where advertising budgets were under pressure. I also brought product habits into the work, from testing newer outreach methods to looking for gaps in what we were offering.

Sponsors were wonderfully direct about value. They wanted to know who would show up, whether the conversations would matter, and how they could justify another year of spending. Sometimes the answer was that they liked us and still could not justify the cost. Those conversations have stayed with me more than any abstract lecture about monetization.

I grew revenue in the business I was working from compared with the prior period, but the broader organization remained under budget pressure. The sales positions were eliminated in November 2025. It was another abrupt ending to a chapter I had entered deliberately. By then, though, I had started to see an industry problem I could not stop thinking about.

My first impression was how different the environment felt. I had moved from young software teams into an organization with nearly two centuries of institutional history. There were relationships that had lasted longer than my entire professional career. There were expectations about advertising and sponsorships shaped by years of experience, even as the market around publishing and events was changing. It was humbling to become new at something again.

I started without an inherited book of prospects and had to build relationships in a crowded market. The work involved far more than making a pitch. A sponsor might need a package that included print, digital, events, and specific onsite deliverables. Contracts had to be coordinated. Activation details had to be clear. Someone had to ensure that the thing promised in the sales conversation could be delivered by the people producing the event or publication. I worked across roughly sixty-three client relationships and a calendar that included fifty-two annual live events in the broader program, according to my résumé records.

I learned to hear a customer objection differently. 'We don't have budget' can mean several things. A company may genuinely be short on cash. The buyer may not understand how a sponsorship will influence the outcome they care about. They may have supported the same thing for years without being able to explain its value to leadership. Sometimes they simply do not need the thing you are selling. Each of those realities calls for a different response.

That experience challenged habits I had acquired on the product side. It is easy for a team to feel proud of a feature because it is elegant, useful, and difficult to build. The person signing a purchase order has to make a different calculation. What problem does this solve? Why now? What evidence could I bring to my boss? What will change if I buy it? The best product teams understand those questions before asking sales to do all the explaining.

I brought a product manager's curiosity into the job. I looked at the tools we used, investigated ways to communicate more effectively, and tried to understand which parts of the offer were changing with the market. I had to learn the disciplines of prospecting, account management, negotiation, and a revenue number that did not care how much effort I had spent on the week. My book of business grew revenue compared with the prior period despite the difficult market.

That role is a central part of why I care about commercial viability now. It gave me direct experience being the person who had to earn the customer's yes and then help deliver on what had been promised. I left with far more respect for salespeople and a much sharper understanding of how much better product and sales can be when they are listening to one another.

sections.title: I wanted the internet to feel like friends again
sections.subtitle: Spring 2025 onward · Bridger
sections.preview: I miss parts of the older internet. Not everything about it. There was plenty of nonsense. But there was a feeling that a social account belonged to a person rather than to an audience-development strategy. I didn't want my friends to become content creators just to remain visible in one another's lives. Bridger came out of that frustration, and out of a fairly stubborn belief that technology can help people be better friends without demanding all their attention.
sections.expanded:
I have always loved bringing people together. I made posters for students in high school because I wanted them to feel noticed. I worked on events because I wanted a crowd to have a shared experience. I kept thinking about what technology could do for friendship because I had seen how the platforms that were once built around friends were becoming something else. Friends had been replaced by feeds, personal updates by content strategies, and genuine closeness by the incentives to grow an audience.

Bridger began as a response to that frustration. I imagined a social app that understood different levels of closeness, where the people closest to you had more room in your experience than a distant acquaintance or a public figure. My planning explored an Inner Circle, broader friends, and people you had just met. That structure mattered to me because a relationship is not simply a follow button. Real people do not experience every connection as equal, and a useful social product should respect that.

I became particularly excited about scrapbooks. I love the idea that people can preserve a day together without treating it as a public performance. A page could hold photographs, a little bit of writing, audio, places, and the people who were there. Friends could create things together and eventually turn their digital memories into something tangible. I began thinking about groups for clubs, communities, families, and people organizing real experiences.
