Those ideas expanded into a product that might let different communities choose the features they need.

The business model matters too. I have explored a cooperative structure and membership dues because I do not want the incentives of the product to depend on maximizing the number of minutes someone spends staring at it. The goal is a more satisfying relationship with social technology and more reasons to leave the app to do something with people. It is an ambitious goal, and many of its components remain plans or development work rather than finished features.

Building Bridger has demanded decisions across mobile software, onboarding, design systems, privacy, authentication, analytics, and the difficult business of giving someone a simple experience with complex infrastructure behind it. I have worked with React and React Native, backend services, databases, and external tools. My role has combined product management and hands-on technical work with coordination of collaborators. My résumé has also recorded early community participation around the project, but I want any public claim about users, volunteers, or release status to match the current verified product state when this page goes live.

Bridger is personal in a way that most products are not. I would love to build a place that makes it easier for someone to reach out to an old friend, preserve a memory, find a community, or spend a little less of their day performing for strangers. My childhood obsession with imagined worlds has become a very practical question: what should the digital spaces we live in feel like?

sections.title: The second layoff brought a question home
sections.subtitle: November 2025 · An unexpected ending and a new problem
sections.preview: Being laid off once is disorienting. Having it happen again, after deliberately changing roles to learn something new, is a different kind of discouraging. I knew the decision wasn't a referendum on every hour I'd worked, but I still had to live with the practical consequences. I also had a year's worth of unusually direct exposure to what event sponsors wanted, what organizers struggled with, and what attendees hoped would happen when they walked into a room.
sections.expanded:
I had chosen the sales role because I wanted to understand a commercial problem from the inside. I got what I wanted, although the ending was nothing like I had hoped. Advertising and events were facing pressure from budgets, changing expectations, and the difficulty of demonstrating results. We worked hard to build business in that environment. When the company decided to eliminate the sales positions, I had no control over the decision.

That made for an uncomfortable career chronology. I had loved Crew and lost the role when funding was tight. I had chosen sales on purpose and lost that role during an organizational reduction. A person skimming dates could easily conclude that I had been bouncing between unrelated jobs. I knew why I had made the choices, what I had built, and how much I had learned, but I was exhausted by the idea of trying to condense all that into three bullet points.

Still, one conversation from the sales job kept replaying in my head. Sponsors wanted more than their logo on a banner. They wanted to meet people who mattered to the business and have some reason to believe the investment had produced something useful. Attendees often wanted to meet a particular kind of person, yet most were left to mingle by chance. Organizers wanted the community to be excited, the event to feel worthwhile, and the results to justify doing it again. Everybody had something they were hoping for, and the software often seemed better at administering registrations than at helping those outcomes happen.

I had been teaching myself about modern AI outside of work, partly because I worried that a deliberate period in sales would leave me behind technically. At first I built small experiments to understand the tools. The more I learned about language models, embeddings, structured data, and agents, the more I thought about how they might help people navigate an event with greater intention.

The layoff gave me space to work seriously on the idea. I could have chosen to view that transition only as another interruption. I was more interested in whether I could turn what I had learned from sales and product into a system that made introductions more useful and outcomes more visible. It became the starting point for Intro.

sections.title: I started building an AI teammate for live events
sections.subtitle: Late 2025 onward · Intro
sections.preview: At a conference, everybody tells you networking is important. Then they send you into a room full of people wearing name badges and hope for the best. I kept wondering why we were still doing that. A person might have traveled across the country because they needed to meet a particular kind of collaborator, customer, or mentor. The person could be standing ten feet away, and neither would know it. Intro started there, with a question that sounded simple enough to be dangerous.
sections.expanded:
I had been teaching myself the modern AI stack at night because I did not want to leave product work for a year and return technically out of date. That became useful very quickly. I moved from experiments with LLM APIs to building real application flows using model providers, embeddings, vector search, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Supabase, and the web stack around them. I have worked on onboarding, event data models, matching explanations, privacy boundaries, and analytics that measure whether a recommendation led to a meaningful introduction.

The questions get harder as the product becomes more agentic. What is the system allowed to change? Which event details have to remain locked because an organizer approved them? How does an AI-generated recommendation become understandable to a human being? How do we keep one organization’s data separate from another’s? I spend a lot of time thinking about trust and permissions because a charming interface means very little if the information behind it is wrong.

I have been speaking with organizers and university stakeholders, testing what they need and designing small pilots. Some capabilities exist in working software; others remain prototypes or roadmap ideas. I want the product to be useful to an organizer running a modest event, with the possibility of helping a community stay connected after everybody goes home.

I have learned how to use AI as a building tool while being clear about where it is brittle. It has let me do work I could not have attempted alone a few years ago. It has also made me appreciate experienced engineering judgment more, because every shortcut eventually becomes somebody’s problem to maintain.

The challenge has always seemed deeply human to me. Most people do not arrive at a conference wanting to collect a hundred contacts they will never speak to again. They may want a mentor, a first customer, a collaborator, a new friend, or the one person who understands a problem they have been working on for months. An organizer cannot personally understand every attendee's hopes and connect every pair, especially once an event grows. But technology could help by making those intentions more visible and by suggesting introductions with a reason behind them.

I began by structuring the information people volunteered during onboarding: their goals, industries, interests, what they could offer, and what they hoped to find. I explored embeddings and vector search as one part of matching, while keeping the human meaning of the recommendation central. A similarity score can help narrow possibilities, but people need to understand why another person is worth approaching. I wanted suggestions that could explain themselves in ordinary language instead of asking an attendee to trust a mysterious number.

Intro taught me that an AI product includes far more than a model call. I worked directly with LLM APIs, Postgres and vector storage, Supabase, backend architecture, authentication, and frontend work in Next.js, React, and TypeScript. I had to learn how different kinds of data should be structured, how to protect identifiable information, and how to design workflows where an agent can recommend an action without accidentally overstepping its authority. I have worked on privacy and governance approaches, including avoiding direct PII in model inputs and considering institutional requirements for data separation.

The product has been changing as I learned more from organizers. A matchmaking feature is only one part of a live event. Somebody needs an agenda that matches the actual event. Sponsors want evidence of meaningful engagement. Organizers need answers to questions from attendees, updates to details, maps, clear communication, and a record of what happened. I began to see Intro as a teammate that could help build and operate those experiences, using approved tools and an authoritative event record rather than inventing its own version of reality.

That shift also made me more interested in generative interfaces. Every gathering is a little different. A small community event should not have to navigate the same enormous software menu as a major conference. I want the software to adapt within safe boundaries to what the organizer is trying to accomplish. That requires an unusual combination of product design, technical constraints, permissions, and careful decisions about which components can be generated and which parts of an event are fixed.

I have worked with potential customers and university stakeholders, including conversations around an event use case at UVU, and moved through prototypes, pilots, and ongoing iteration. I am careful about the distinction between what has been demonstrated, what is being built, and what remains a plan. I want Intro to be able to support organizers in practice, and I want the claims about it to be as dependable as the system we are trying to create.

I love this work because the technology disappears into the human outcome when it succeeds. Someone walks away from an event having met the person they came to find. An organizer spends less of the day worrying about logistics and more time caring for the people there. A sponsor can point to a real conversation rather than a vague impression. That is the kind of AI product I want to keep building.

sections.title: I decided I needed to understand the machinery
sections.subtitle: 2025 to 2026 · Learning to build with AI
sections.preview: I don't want to be the person in a meeting who says 'AI could do that' and then leaves the actual engineering as somebody else's problem. I have been that close to technology long enough to know that describing a feature is not the same as understanding what it takes to build it. So I started doing more of the building myself. It has meant a lot of debugging, rethinking assumptions, and discovering that a confident-looking software demo can conceal an alarming number of edge cases.
sections.expanded:
My technical curiosity did not begin with AI. I had written spreadsheets and dashboards in England, worked on analytics instrumentation at Divvy, and coordinated financial infrastructure at Crew. I had watched engineers solve problems for years and learned enough to have useful conversations with them. But there is a different kind of education in being the person whose code breaks and realizing nobody else is scheduled to fix it.

I began experimenting with chatbots, model APIs, structured prompts, and small tools. As the tooling improved, I learned frontend and backend concepts more directly. I have spent time in React and TypeScript, with Postgres, Supabase, cloud services, and development tools that let me move from an idea to something I can put in front of a user. Every week seems to introduce a new way to build, and I have had to learn to judge those possibilities against the customer problem instead of chasing every announcement.

The most interesting technical lessons have involved reliability. A model can produce a beautiful answer and still misunderstand what it is authorized to change. A workflow can appear clever until a user changes one field and the agent silently rewrites three things that were already settled. I have become increasingly interested in permissions, locked decisions, audit trails, data provenance, and the separation between what an agent proposes and what it is allowed to execute. Those constraints are product decisions as much as engineering decisions.

I have also learned the limits of building alone. I can make an impressive amount of progress by studying the system and asking modern tools to help, but there is no substitute for specialized judgment. A strong engineer can see risks I have missed. A designer can make a system much easier to understand. Security, compliance, and product economics all benefit from someone who has worked in the discipline long enough to recognize the subtle mistakes. I enjoy becoming more technical precisely because it makes those conversations richer.

There is a temptation in AI to describe everything as a revolution, and I understand the excitement. What matters to me is whether the result works. I want to know what the person was trying to do, what the product knew, why it took an action, whether it respected the user's instructions, and how we verified the outcome. I have spent years moving between people and systems. AI has made that work faster and far more interesting, but the responsibility has not gone away.

sections.title: The civic part of my brain never stopped asking questions
sections.subtitle: 2026 onward · Civic projects and public ideas
sections.preview: My interest in government has been wandering around in the background of my life for years, periodically interrupting whatever else I am supposed to be doing. I read about electoral systems, legislative design, and the various ways societies try to let people disagree without making the whole enterprise impossible. The questions can sound very abstract until I remember the people waiting on grant applications or constituent services. Institutions aren't just diagrams. Somebody has to live with the result.
sections.expanded:
A few of my earliest experiences made me unusually attentive to the distance between a person's problem and the system responsible for helping. I had sat with city staff and watched how slow a simple improvement could be. I had helped business owners make sense of grant rules during COVID. I had listened to constituent concerns in Washington. Each experience taught me how much people want to be heard, especially when a system feels impossible to influence.

I also care about what happens when people begin to assume nothing can change. The sentence I heard while trying to build the Resilience Arch still bothers me: nothing like this ever gets done. That mentality is understandable. People have been disappointed, ignored, and exhausted by processes that ask them to participate while giving them little evidence that participation matters. I have seen enough small groups accomplish unlikely things to be unwilling to accept that as the final answer.

I have explored ways to make civic conversation more accessible, including an idea for small groups where people can describe their values, hear a different perspective, and learn where there is genuine agreement or disagreement. I am interested in tools that help a facilitator manage equal speaking time, summarize what people meant, and separate an unresolved difference from a misunderstanding. Technology should make it easier for ordinary people to participate without requiring a policy degree or a talent for arguing on television.

I write about democratic structures, public institutions, and what better participation might look like. Some of those ideas are ambitious and unfinished. I am comfortable admitting that. I would rather develop them in conversation with people who know what I do not than announce a grand solution. The creative work is in making a difficult system legible enough that more people can contribute to improving it.

That civic interest belongs in the same life story as my product career. The projects may have different audiences, but I keep returning to experiences that are too confusing, closed, or indifferent to the people they are supposed to serve. I care deeply about whether we can make them better and whether more people can take part in doing it.

sections.title: I am still a creator, even when I am deep in code
sections.subtitle: Now · Building, writing, and working with people
sections.preview: I sometimes look at the things I want to make and wonder whether I should pick one kind of person to be. A product manager? A writer? A performer? A founder? Someone who spends an unreasonable amount of time thinking about civic institutions? The trouble is that I like all of those activities. They don't all need to become careers. Some things are worth doing because making them is part of being alive.
sections.expanded:
My work on the Resilience Arch and the scholarship began with who gets recognized. The government internships taught me what public systems look like from inside them. The civic projects I am exploring now ask a related question: what would make it easier for more people to participate, listen, disagree productively, and see where there is common ground?

I am interested in the tools as much as the ideals. Facilitation, accessible language, transparent decisions, privacy, and the ability to include people who cannot spend their evenings reading policy papers are design problems. I like working on problems where a technically elegant system would still fail if it forgot the humans using it.

I do some writing about these ideas too. I know I will change my mind about parts of them as I learn. That feels like a good reason to keep listening.

I still want to perform. I still want to write work that helps people feel understood or see an idea differently. I enjoy design, and I love putting something visual together in a way that feels considered. I get excited about maps, events, architecture, and the way a room changes when people are invited to participate. I cannot imagine becoming so narrowly professional that those interests have to disappear.

Some of the most useful things I have learned came from disciplines that a recruiter might not immediately associate with product management. Theater taught me what coordinated excellence feels like and what happens when the audience doesn't get the experience you intended. Government taught me about constraints, stakeholders, and the difference between someone's stated request and their underlying need. Sales taught me what it means when a buyer cannot justify the cost. Financial technology taught me to respect regulation, vendor dependencies, and the hidden infrastructure that makes a feature possible. Building my own applications taught me what it feels like to own the bug at midnight.

I write because my interests often begin as a question I cannot stop thinking about. Sometimes the subject is AI or software. Other times it is loneliness, community, public institutions, art, or the peculiar ways people organize their lives. I would like to publish more of the work rather than letting perfectionism keep it in drafts. I do not want every thought to arrive with a personal branding strategy. I want the writing to be useful and feel like a human being was thinking on the page.

The work that excites me most still has people at its center. I love being in a room with specialists who know different things, helping everyone understand the same problem, and watching their contributions become something none of them would have made in quite the same way alone. I also like that a team can make room for humor and imagination even when the problem is technically difficult. A serious product should not require everyone building it to become humorless.

sections.title: What I want to do with the years ahead
sections.subtitle: Now and what comes next · Product, creativity, and collaboration
sections.preview: I don't have a five-year plan that accounts for every turn. I have a set of things I keep returning to: build something useful, work with people who care, create more than I consume, take public life seriously, and not postpone all the fun until some imaginary future in which everything is finally settled. I'm ambitious. I can also be impatient, get lost in the planning, and start something new before the last thing has been properly finished. All of that belongs in the story too.
sections.expanded:
The practical toolkit is broad. I work with product discovery, customer interviews, requirements, prioritization, experiments, analytics, SQL and Python, design tools, and the software stack behind AI applications. I am comfortable reading code, discussing APIs and databases, looking at a funnel, talking through a go-to-market problem, and asking a designer to show me what is confusing about the flow. I have learned each of those things in places where the work needed to move forward.

My favorite teams resemble theater companies. People have different specialties, and the experience belongs to all of them. A product manager has to keep the customer and the whole system visible, especially when a perfectly sensible decision in one department causes a problem in another.

I would love to return to the Washington, D.C. area and contribute to a company doing ambitious, useful work. I am particularly interested in products where technology meets human behavior and where the commercial and technical realities are taken as seriously as the design. I like complicated environments. I also like people who can laugh when a complicated environment does something ridiculous.

I still have the same instinct I had when I was making posters for students at my high school. If something good could happen, I want to find out what it would take to make it happen. The older I get, the more I appreciate how many people it takes to do that well.

I have held enough different roles to understand why a simple job title often fails to describe the work. At Crew, being a Senior Product Manager meant talking to financial partners about program requirements one day and making an illustration system work the next. In sales, being an account executive meant learning the economics of an industry and hearing the concerns of the people who were expected to pay for the product. As a founder, my tasks have ranged from customer interviews to debugging application behavior, privacy decisions, positioning, and the awkward business of persuading someone to give a new idea their time.

That breadth can be misunderstood, and I understand why. A résumé is designed to help a stranger identify a pattern quickly. Mine asks for a little more context. But I have been moving toward the same kind of work for a long time: find something worth improving, understand the people involved, learn the systems, and bring the right crafts together to do it well. Product management has become the clearest home for that combination.

I value ambition. I want to help create things large enough to matter. I also know that a big idea cannot compensate for poor judgment, a fragile system, or a team that does not trust one another. I have watched a company struggle with financing after a launch. I have dealt with customer objections that exposed weaknesses in an offer. I have seen a good design become complicated by regulation and manufacturing constraints. I have learned that the best response is to get closer to the facts and work with people who understand what you do not.

I am also less interested now in proving I can do everything myself. I have done a surprising amount of independent building, and I am proud of it. What I miss most when working alone is the moment when another person's talent changes the direction of the work for the better. I love designers who see things I cannot see, engineers who find an elegant solution, researchers who challenge the plan, and colleagues who are willing to disagree constructively because they care about the result.

Washington remains somewhere I would love to build a life and career. The city first captured my imagination as a teenager, and the time I spent working there showed me how energizing it is to be around people who care intensely about the things they are doing. I want a team with that quality of curiosity and commitment, wherever the work leads. I want hard problems, a healthy appetite for experimentation, an honest relationship with evidence, and the chance to help others do the best work of their careers.

I sometimes think back to my dad's answer about how he would spend his last day. I am not ready to give the same answer, but I would like to be moving toward it. I want to make things, make a contribution, care well for the people around me, and look back on a life in which the work had some meaning beyond my title. There are still a great many ideas I want to try. I hope I get to try them with people I admire.
